title: My experience with Gdevelope + Claude Code so far.
author: smokalone
selftext:
Hi everyone! I’m writing this post to share the pros and cons of my current GDevelop workflow and to get some tips on how to improve it.

I currently have a Claude Pro account and I’m using **Sonnet 4.6** to edit the game's JSON files directly (I find the built-in engine AI a bit "clunky" and it tends to generate too many bugs). My plan is to build all the core mechanics first, so I can easily focus on creating scenes and dialogue for my 2D top-down RPG whenever I have some free time.

I chose GDevelop because it’s free and cross-platform; I love being able to open the app on my phone and tweak a scene whenever I have a spare minute.

**Since starting, here’s my take so far:**

* **Pros:** It’s a very convenient combo. I can create complex objects quickly and then "assemble" the game in GDevelop as if it were a sandbox—it’s almost like a game within a game.
* **Cons:** It’s not exactly "free" considering the AI costs, and the Claude Pro limitations are quite tedious. For example, Sonnet often requires multiple iterations for significant changes. On the other hand, if I try using **Opus**, a single prompt can hit the token limit, forcing me to wait 5 hours for a reset (which is frustrating because token usage feels so unpredictable).

Does anyone have any advice on how to optimize this workflow or suggest any alternatives? Thanks!

comments.author: daddywookie
comments.body:
A fellow GDevelop enjoyer!

I've been building up a skill for GDevelop which I am finding really helps with creating accurate JSON. I started it in Claude and now use it with Codex.

[https://github.com/adamboothuk/gdevelop-reference](https://github.com/adamboothuk/gdevelop-reference)

It's still a work in progress but the core is there. I'm currently working through creating objects and all of the extensions and behaviours. It can understand scenes, external events, layouts and many other aspects of the engine.

One very useful addition is that it can also set up external logging so you can have it create log outputs and send them to a file locally. It really helps with debugging.

This is my first public repo so apologies if it is not super optimised but it might help you out. There are likely still some local file references in there

replies.author: daddywookie
replies.body:
I'd be really interested if it makes a difference if you feed it into Claude. It might help give Sonnet a bit of a boost and cut down on token usage. I've no idea how you would test it but to be honest, even a confirmation that it doesn't break anything would give me confidence to continue.

I also made sure that I got Codex to build me an [architecture.md](http://architecture.md) file so it knows where to find certain features of my game. It's a bit of an upfront cost but a long term saving.

replies.author: smokalone
replies.body: thats interesting, im a bit new to claud but ill try this method and give an update. The more i features i generate for the game, the more tokens requires even for small bugs ahah

replies.author: daddywookie
replies.body:
Yeah, it can be a heavy load as the files get long. I've found it important to break up long scenes and use external events more. Then with a good architecture.md file Claude can focus on only the important files.

It also helps if you can tell the agent where to look. I use event groups and comments a lot to clearly describe what is happening and to be able to tell the agent where to find the code I'm working on.

replies.author: daddywookie
replies.body: I tried throwing the logging setup at Claude and it made some suggestions. I've just pushed an update into the reop that contains more solid examples of how to set up the logging so Claude should be able to handle it better.

comments.author: morewordsfaster
comments.body: It's difficult to provide much help without knowing the kinds of prompts you're using, but I would guess that's the reason why you are hitting token limits so quickly. I'm using Opus and haven't really had any problems, but I'm very specific and tightly scoped with my prompts and I am careful to balance usage across Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku. Opus I mainly use just for planning, then I switch to Sonnet or Haiku for implementation.
